newsitem.title: USA: Bio-Vascular sees female product trials.
newsitem.headline: Bio-Vascular sees female product trials.

text.p: Bio-Vascular Inc said Tuesday that, if all goes well, it expects to begin human clinical trials by the fall of 1998 on a product for the surgical treatment of female urinary stress incontinence.
"Over the long term, we have a number of opportunities that could result in a quantum leap in our revenue," said president and chief executive Karen Gilles.
For the third quarter ended July 31, the company reported net revenue of $2.4 million, about five percent below revenue of $2.5 million for the third quarter last year.

The decline was due in large part to a 42 percent drop in sales of Peri-Strips, which went to $594,000 from $1 million. Offsetting that decline was a gain in sales of Tissue-Guard products other than Peri-Strips to $1.1 million from $757,000.

"Peri-Strips revenue for the quarter was affected primarily by distributors working down their inventory in anticipation of...new product and fewer cases of lung volume reduction (LVR) surgery because hospitals are not promoting the procedure as aggressively," Gilles said.

The company reported a loss from continuing operations of $491,000 for the quarter. Of that total, $300,000 was a non-operating loss from the write-off of a tax benefit which the company will be unable to use. In the third quarter last year, Bio-Vascular had income from continuing operations of $111,000, and a loss from discontinued operations of $288,000, for a total net loss of $177,000.
Gross margin improved in the quarter, up two points to 60 percent, the company said.

Operating expenses increased, however, mainly as the result of one-time costs related to the resignation of the company's former chief executive, costs for the company's effort to secure reimbursement for LVR surgery for Medicare beneficiaries, and higher selling expenses related to the launch of Peri-Strips Dry, a new product, Bio-Vascular said.

The tax benefit write-off relates to operating loss carryforwards that the company had previously expected to use in its current fiscal year. Because a federal study of LVR surgery, originally expected to begin in June, will not start until January 1998 at the earliest, the company will not have the product revenue from the study, and the resulting earnings, that would have allowed the use of these carryforwards in the permitted time period, it said.
